newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's CDU wants VAT hike to help cut wage costs.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's CDU wants VAT hike to help cut wage costs.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrat (CDU) said on Saturday they supported discussions on a rise in valued added tax (VAT) which could help to reduce supplemental wage costs as well as fund a tax reform.

Peter Hintze, general secretary of the CDU, told a news conference at the end of a two-day party leadership meeting that the CDU would discuss how to use the funds once the government tax and pension commissions make their proposals.

The CDU position contrasted with that of its sister party in Bavaria, the Christian Social Union (CSU), which argues a rise in VAT should be to fund the government's planned sweeping tax reform from 1999 but should not be used for other purposes.
When asked whether the CDU would consider reducing supplemental wage costs at the same time as introducing the planned tax reform, Hintze replied: "Yes", but gave no further details.
Hintze said that during the meeting held in the village of Windhagen just outside Bonn, Kohl had said any increase in VAT would not take place before general elections in 1998.

A VAT hike, which many economists consider a near certainty, would be the government's last resort after first trying to plug gaps in financing by chopping billions in tax deductions for businesses and private individuals.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Wednesday the government might have to raise VAT and taxes on pensions in order to finance planned cuts of up to 30 billion marks ($19 billion) in income taxes.

Hintze said the CDU would start to discuss whether a VAT hike was needed and what the revenue generated should be used for after the government tax commission meets on Wednesday and after the pension committee meets in the near future.
Supplemental wage costs are paid partly by employers and partly by employees. They include unemployument benefit and health insurance contributions.

Kohl's CDU also dismissed once again demands from junior coalition partner the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) to set a date for the abolition of the solidarity tax surcharge -- an issue that has been at the centre of a coalition dispute.
"The CDU is not prepared to decide yet when to do away with the solidarity surcharge because of the present economic data," Hintze said, referring to economic figures from east Germany.

The CSU and CDU argue that the solidarity tax -- a 7.5 percent income tax surcharge -- brings in around 30 billion marks in revenue each year and could not be abolished without secure financing for east Germany.
Kohl's centre-right coalition government has agreed to cut the tax to 5.5 percent next year but the FDP is demanding it be scrapped completely by around 2000.
